paper_metadata.title: Autocallable Options Pricing with Integration-Based Exponential Amplitude Loading

summary: The paper proposes an improved integration‑based exponential amplitude loading method for quantum derivative pricing and analytically shows the payoff module T‑depth can drop from about 2.1×10^3 to about 40 (≈50× reduction). The authors implement an end‑to‑end autocallable option pricing circuit and validate it via simulators up to 33 qubits, demonstrating convergence toward classical Monte Carlo estimates as discretization and arithmetic precision increase.

experiments.description: Gate-based quantum simulation and validation of an autocallable option pricing circuit using integration-based exponential amplitude loading, implemented in Qmod/Classiq and executed on simulators/HPC for a single-asset, 3-time-step, 2-binary-option instance.

algorithm.variant: Autocallable option pricing with integration-based exponential amplitude loading and iterative QAE
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Iterative QAE used to estimate the target-qubit probability; paper reports target confidence level with ϵ = 0.001 and α = 0.002
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Gaussian state preparation from standard normal distribution; no trainable variational parameters reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Standard Gaussian distributions are loaded for each time step; log-returns are accumulated in an m-qubit register; binary conditions are checked with comparators; payoff is encoded into a target qubit amplitude via controlled Ry rotations and integration-based exponential amplitude loading
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate the expected discounted payoff of an autocallable option by measuring the target qubit probability and rescaling it to the payoff domain
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Path-dependent conditions handled by comparators and indicator registers for binary knock-out events and barrier crossing; put payoff loaded only if no binary triggered and barrier was crossed

problem_instance.description: Single-asset autocallable option with three monitoring time steps and two binary options expiring at the first two monitoring points; includes a short knock-in put at maturity

dataset_specification.description: Model parameters given in Table II; no market dataset named

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Classical benchmark comparisons use Monte Carlo, Monte Carlo with the same Gaussian discretization, closed form with Gaussian discretization, and closed form with Gaussian discretization plus fixed-point precision
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Quantum circuits synthesized and executed on exact shot-based simulators; configurations run on Classiq default simulator, Nvidia simulator, and LEONARDO HPC/Cirq simulator; results compared against classical benchmarks and convergence illustrated across increasing qubit precision/discretization

hardware.provider: Classiq simulator; NVIDIA GPU simulator; Cirq simulator with cuQuantum on the LEONARDO HPC system (CINECA)

implementation_details.transpilation_target: Classiq synthesized gate-based circuit; width minimized for simulator execution
implementation_details.classical_solver: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) used for estimation; classical baselines include Monte Carlo and closed-form calculations
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Gaussian discretization and fixed-point precision settings varied to match quantum circuit constraints
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Rescaling from amplitude probability to payoff using normalization factor fmax + (K - rTmin)V; comparison to classical benchmarks

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: Convergence to classical benchmark shown as qubit precision increases; no optimizer loss curve

speedup_claims.conditions: using quantum amplitude estimation; query complexity O(1/epsilon) versus O(1/epsilon^2)
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the quadratic speedup in theory; the experiments are simulator-based validation rather than a hardware demonstration of speedup.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: prior integration-based amplitude loading method / state-of-the-art payoff component
speedup_claims.conditions: relevant setting for the payoff component T-depth analysis
speedup_claims.caveats: This is an analytical T-depth comparison, not an end-to-end runtime measurement.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/ϵ) for QAE estimation; circuit T-depth analyzed as a function of Gaussian preparation, arithmetic, exponential loading, and IQAE calls
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: Analytically reduced payoff-component T-depth by ~50x relative to prior method in a relevant setting

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not quantified; advantage discussed asymptotically via QAE vs Monte Carlo scaling
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires fault‑tolerant quantum computers with large logical qubit counts and low T-depth circuits; current demonstrations limited to ≤33 qubits in classical simulation
limiting_factors: Experiments executed only on classical simulators, not real QPUs
Small proof‑of‑concept instance (1 asset, 3 time steps)
Large circuit size even for small instances
Amplitude loading and arithmetic modules dominate T-depth
Quadratic speedup (QAE vs Monte Carlo) insufficient to overcome error‑correction overhead

notes: 33 qubits is explicitly stated as the maximum experiment size on LEONARDO HPC.
Hardware is simulator-based; no real QPU is used.
The paper reports T-depth analytically and gives a specific payoff-component reduction (~2.1e3 to ~40), but not a full compiled circuit depth or gate counts.
The paper claims potential quadratic speedup via Quantum Amplitude Estimation relative to Monte Carlo but does not experimentally demonstrate quantum advantage.
All results are simulator-based validations of correctness and convergence rather than performance superiority.
